summary: Hebrew has ten subject pronouns. In the second and third person they show gender in the singular and in the plural: אַתָּה “you” to a man, אַתְּ to a woman; הוּא “he”, הִיא “she”; אַתֶּם / אַתֶּן “you (pl.)”; הֵם / הֵן “they”. A group with at least one man takes the masculine plural. There is no “it” (a thing is הוּא or הִיא by its gender) and no polite “you”. In the present tense the pronoun is required, because the verb shows only gender and number; in the past and future the verb ending already shows the person, so the pronoun is often left out.

blocks.caption: The subject pronouns. The first person has no gender: אֲנִי and אֲנַחְנוּ are said by men and women alike.

blocks.text: The pronoun stands first, and in the present the rest of the sentence follows directly — there is no verb “am / are / is”: אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְט “I am a student”, הִיא מוֹרָה “she is a teacher”, הֵם חֲבֵרִים “they are friends”.

items.title: To one person
points: a man or boy → אַתָּה: אַתָּה מוֹרֶה
a woman or girl → אַתְּ: אַתְּ מוֹרָה
the same for a friend, a stranger or a minister

items.title: To several people
points: men, or men and women → אַתֶּם: אַתֶּם חֲבֵרִים
one man in the group → אַתֶּם

blocks.title: No “it”
blocks.text: Things are “he” or “she” by their gender: הַסֵּפֶר? הוּא פֹּה “the book? it is here” (סֵפֶר is masculine); הַמְּנוֹרָה? הִיא שָׁם (מְנוֹרָה is feminine). For a situation, or when you point at something, Hebrew uses זֶה (lesson 3).

blocks.title: Look-alike words
blocks.text: Without vowels, אַתְּ “you (f.)” is written את — exactly like the object marker אֶת of lesson 7; הוּא and הִיא differ only in ו / י. אַתָּה ends in a silent ה.

blocks.title: For your languages
blocks.text: German du / Sie, Russian ты / вы and Greek εσύ / εσείς have a polite “you”; Hebrew does not — but it has the gender split that English, German and Russian lack in “you”.

blocks.title: Ask yourself before choosing the pronoun
questions: Who is it: me, the person I talk to, or someone else?
A man, a woman, or a mixed group?
Is it a thing? Then: is the noun masculine or feminine?

askYourself: Am I talking about myself (אֲנִי / אֲנַחְנוּ), to someone (אַתָּה / אַתְּ / אַתֶּם / אַתֶּן) or about someone (הוּא / הִיא / הֵם / הֵן)?
One person or more than one?
Is it a man or a woman — and for a group, is there at least one man? (Then masculine plural.)
Is it a thing? Then use הוּא or הִיא by the noun’s gender — there is no “it”.
Is the sentence in the present? Then keep the pronoun; in the past or future it can be dropped.
steps: Put the pronoun first; in the present add the noun or place directly.

traps: אַתְּ (to a woman) vs אַתָּה (to a man): the most common beginner mistake is to use אַתָּה for everyone.
A mixed group is masculine: אַתֶּם, הֵם — even if most of them are women.
There is no “it”: *זֶה הוּא פֹּה is wrong for “it is here”; say הוּא פֹּה (for a masculine thing).
There is no polite form: do not look for a “Sie” — אַתָּה / אַתְּ is polite enough with בְּבַקָּשָׁה.
Do not insert a verb “to be” after the pronoun: אֲנִי מוֹרֶה, not *אֲנִי הוּא מוֹרֶה.

seeAlso.note: The same system with gender in “you”: أَنْتَ (to a man) / أَنْتِ (to a woman), هُوَ / هِيَ — and Arabic adds dual pronouns (أَنْتُمَا, هُمَا).
German has a neuter es “it” and a polite Sie, but no gender in “you”; Hebrew has gendered “you” and neither es nor Sie.
Chinese 他 / 她 / 它 are all pronounced tā — gender only in writing; the plural is made with 们 (我们, 你们, 他们).
